MSK–SKIN · WEEK 13 · LECTURE 7

Vertebral Column & Back

Full lecture companion · Morganne Manuel, Ph.D. · Anatomy-first teaching with original lecture figures and selective clinical bridges

Objectives1. Overview, regions, and v2. The vertebral building b3. Joints and ligament rest4. Intervertebral discs, he5. Pathology and imaging6. Vessels and sensory inne7. Superficial and intermed8. Deep intrinsic muscles

Official learning objectives · all seven

  1. Identify the normal structure/function of vertebral column, joints and ligaments.
  2. Differentiate five vertebral regions and parts of typical vertebra.
  3. Distinguish normal spinal curvatures and kyphosis, lordosis, scoliosis.
  4. Explain disc components/function and herniation implications.
  5. Explain anatomical basis of spondylosis, spondylolisthesis and vertebral injuries.
  6. Identify superficial/deep back muscle attachments, innervation, blood supply, actions and testing.
  7. Identify back/vertebral structures on X-ray, MRI and CT.

Big picture

First identify the bone, then the joint or ligament, then the nerve at risk, then the movement lost. The same map works in the gross anatomy lab, the clinic, and imaging.

01Overview, regions, and vertebral curvatures

The vertebral column has four linked jobs: support body weight, protect neural tissue, allow controlled motion, and dampen axial forces. Each region changes its geometry to meet the local requirements.

RegionCountDistinguishing function/appearance
Cervical7Small bodies, transverse foramina; mobile head/neck
Thoracic12Costal articulations; rib cage support
Lumbar5Large bodies; strong load bearing, flexion/extension
Sacrum5 fusedTransmits load to pelvic girdle
Coccyx3–5 fused (lecture)Terminal attachment and support

Curvature is a structural adaptation

Thoracic and sacral: primary curvatures, concave anteriorly. Cervical and lumbar: secondary curves, concave posteriorly (cervical develops with head lifting, lumbar with standing/walking). These multiple bends increase resilience during upright loading.

PatternFindingSource emphasis
KyphosisExaggerated thoracic posterior convexityDegenerative change, anterior body fractures, posture
LordosisExaggerated lumbar inward curveWeak trunk muscles, obesity, pregnancy
ScoliosisLateral curve with vertebral rotationIdiopathic or congenital abnormalities
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Which abnormal curvature includes vertebral rotation, rather than simply exaggerated sagittal curvature?
Show answer and reasoning

Scoliosis. Rotation distinguishes it from isolated kyphosis or lordosis.

02The vertebral building block and regional differences

Trace load and protection separately: vertebral body transmits compressive force, while the pedicles + laminae form the protective vertebral arch. The stacked vertebral foramina form the canal; paired superior/inferior vertebral notches create the intervertebral foramen through which a spinal nerve exits.

Articular processes form zygapophysial (facet) joints. The pars interarticularis is bone between superior and inferior articular processes: a stress fracture there is spondylolysis.

AreaHow to recognizeMovement implications
Typical cervicalSmall body, transverse foramina, usually bifid spinous processRelatively mobile in multiple planes
C1 (atlas)No body or spinous process; lateral masses, anterior/posterior arches, vertebral artery grooveOccipital condyles sit on superior facets; “yes” nod
C2 (axis)Dens projects upward from C2 bodyPivot for C1 rotation; “no” shake
C7Long palpable spinous processVertebra prominens
ThoracicRib facets on body/transverse process; long descending spineRotation; ribs and joints limit flexion/extension
LumbarLarge body, heavy pedicles, short broad spine, mammillary processesFlexion/extension with limited rotation
SacrumAnterior/posterior foramina, promontory, hiatus, auricular surfaceSacroiliac load transfer; sacral rami exit matching foramina
COMMON CONFUSIONVertebral foramen = central opening of each bone; intervertebral foramen = lateral aperture between adjacent vertebrae for exiting spinal nerves.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · A vertebra has a dens. What is its level, and what movement depends on it?
Show answer and reasoning

C2 (axis). The dens acts as a pivot for rotation of C1 and the head at the atlantoaxial joint.

03Joints and ligament restraints

Intervertebral discs between vertebral bodies are symphyses (secondary cartilaginous joints), whereas zygapophysial facet joints are plane synovial joints. Ligament position predicts which motion is restrained.

StructureWhereMechanical role
Anterior longitudinal ligament (ALL)Anterior to vertebral bodies/discsResists hyperextension
Posterior longitudinal ligament (PLL)Posterior surface of bodies, inside vertebral canalResists posterior disc displacement; weakly limits flexion
Ligamentum flavumBetween adjacent laminaeElastic continuity and resistance to separation
InterspinousBetween neighboring spinous processesChecks flexion
SupraspinousAlong tips of spinous processesChecks flexion
Nuchal ligamentExternal occipital protuberance to C7; merges with supraspinousLimits head/neck flexion, muscle attachment
CLINICAL CONNECTIONRear-end collision → rapid cervical hyperextension (whiplash) → anterior longitudinal ligament may be overstretched or torn.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Which ligament is most directly stressed during hyperextension?
Show answer and reasoning

The anterior longitudinal ligament; it lies across the anterior vertebral bodies.

04Intervertebral discs, herniation, and nerve-root localization

The disc consists of a hydrated gelatinous nucleus pulposus encircled by concentric fibrocartilage annulus fibrosus. This arrangement distributes axial loads while allowing movement. Age-related water and proteoglycan loss reduces cushioning, and annular fissures create opportunities for nuclear material to protrude.

Herniations most often project posterolaterally, where the annulus is comparatively thin and ligament support weaker. A typical lumbar posterolateral L4–L5 disc herniation compresses the traversing L5 root; L5–S1 commonly compresses S1. The professor handout notes C5–C6 tends to affect C6 and C6–C7 affects C7.

DiscTypical affected rootClinical logic
L4–L5L5Traversing root in lateral recess
L5–S1S1Traversing root immediately below disc level
C5–C6C6Cervical root exits above vertebra of its number
C6–C7C7Cervical root-number relationship
EXAM TRAPDo not automatically name the upper vertebral level as the compressed lumbar nerve. A posterolateral L4–L5 disc classically injures L5; foraminal/far-lateral lesions may follow a different rule.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · An L4–L5 posterolateral disc presses on a nerve root. Which is the typical root?
Show answer and reasoning

L5, the traversing root. The L4 root has generally exited via its own intervertebral foramen.

05Pathology and imaging: localize what has failed

Read the imaging using anatomic relationships. Ask whether the problem is a defect in bone, malalignment of vertebral bodies, or loss of space for nerves.

TermAnatomic changeRecognition
SpondylolysisFracture/defect of pars interarticularisOblique radiograph: Scotty dog “collar”
SpondylolisthesisOne vertebral body slips relative to adjacent bodySagittal step-off; often L5 on S1
Spinal stenosisNarrow vertebral canal or intervertebral foraminaMRI/CT: reduced available neural space; disc bulge or bone spurs
SpondylosisDegenerative changes of spineBony/disc/facet aging changes (objective; not independently developed as separate slide topic)
FIRST AID CONNECTIONSpondylolysis means pars defect; spondylolisthesis means slippage. They may coexist but are not interchangeable.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · An adolescent athlete has back pain from repeated extension and a Scotty-dog collar on oblique radiograph. Name the lesion.
Show answer and reasoning

Spondylolysis from pars interarticularis stress fracture; vertebral slippage is a different concept.

06Vessels and sensory innervation

Segmental and cervical arterial branches nourish the vertebrae and supporting structures. Internal vertebral venous plexuses lie inside the canal; external plexuses outside it, with communicating channels. These veins lack valves, so infection or malignant cells may spread along the vertebral venous network.

Recurrent meningeal branches of spinal nerves supply periosteum, the outer annulus of IV discs, vertebral ligaments, and meninges; nearby posterior rami supply facet joints. These innervated structures are potential pain generators, even without nerve-root injury.

CLINICAL CONNECTIONValve-free vertebral plexuses provide an anatomical explanation for hematogenous spread of organisms or tumor cells into the spinal region.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Why can a patient have mechanical vertebral pain without radiating weakness?
Show answer and reasoning

Pain-sensitive periosteum, annulus, ligaments, and facet joints may be irritated without a major motor root lesion.

07Superficial and intermediate back muscles

Extrinsic muscles attach the vertebral skeleton to scapula/upper limb or ribs. To distinguish them, use the movement that fails and the motor nerve that supplies them. The lecture emphasizes action and innervation.

MuscleProximal → distal attachment (course)Principal actionInnervation / vascular clue
TrapeziusOcciput, nuchal ligament, C7–T12 spines → lateral clavicle, acromion, scapular spineScapular elevation / retraction / depression by fibersCN XI motor; C3–C4 proprioception; transverse cervical artery
Latissimus dorsiT6–T12 spinous processes, thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest → intertubercular groove floorArm extension, adduction, medial rotationThoracodorsal nerve and artery
Rhomboid majorT2–T5 spines → medial scapular border inferior to spineScapular retractionDorsal scapular nerve/artery
Rhomboid minorC7–T1 spines → scapular spine at medial borderScapular retractionDorsal scapular nerve/artery
Levator scapulaeC1–C4 transverse processes → superior angle and upper medial scapulaElevates/downwardly rotates scapulaDorsal scapular nerve (handout also C3–C4)
Serratus posterior superiorNuchal ligament, C7–T3 spines → ribs 2–4Rib elevation/proprioceptionIntercostal nerves 2–5
Serratus posterior inferiorT11–L2 spines → ribs 8–12Rib depression/proprioceptionIntercostal nerves 9–12
COMMON CONFUSIONTrapezius is tested by shoulder shrug (CN XI). Rhomboids retract the scapula via the dorsal scapular nerve. Latissimus dorsi moves the humerus via the thoracodorsal nerve.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · A patient cannot shrug one shoulder against resistance. Which nerve and muscle are tested?
Show answer and reasoning

Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) supplying trapezius.

08Deep intrinsic muscles: posture and orientation

The deep (intrinsic) back muscles act directly on the head and vertebral column and are characteristically innervated by posterior rami. Compare this to extrinsic muscle groups supplied through anterior rami or CN XI.

GroupAnatomic patternActions / innervation
Splenius capitis/cervicisPosterior neck; capitis to skull; cervicis toward C1–C3/4 transverse processesBoth sides extend; one side laterally flexes and rotates head to same side; posterior rami
Semispinalis (capitis, cervicis, thoracis)Deep to splenius; long fibers transverse processes toward spines/occiputExtension and contralateral rotation; posterior rami
Erector spinae: iliocostalisMost lateral longitudinal column near rib anglesBoth sides extend; one side laterally flexes; posterior rami
Erector spinae: longissimusIntermediate and generally broadest columnSame extension/lateral flexion functions; posterior rami
Erector spinae: spinalisMost medial near spinous processesSame extension/lateral flexion functions; posterior rami
CLINICAL CONNECTIONThe handout distinguishes ligament sprain from muscle strain. Erector spinae microtears can cause localized low-back pain and protective spasm.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Which intrinsic back muscle family rotates the head to the opposite side?
Show answer and reasoning

Semispinalis; splenius classically rotates to the same side.

MASTER THESE BEFORE MOVING ON

  1. Vertebral geometry predicts region and motion: cervical transverse foramina, thoracic rib facets, lumbar weight-bearing bodies; facet orientation modifies movement.
  2. The root rule depends on location: typical posterolateral lumbar disc herniation affects the traversing root (L4–L5 → L5).
  3. Lesion language: pars fracture (spondylolysis), vertebral displacement (spondylolisthesis), reduced neural space (stenosis).
  4. Nerve → action: CN XI–trapezius shrug; thoracodorsal–latissimus arm motion; dorsal scapular–rhomboid/levator scapulae; posterior rami–intrinsic posture.
  5. Directional reasoning: ALL limits extension, posterior ligaments resist flexion; splenius rotates ipsilaterally, semispinalis contralaterally.

THE MOST USEFUL FIRST AID CONNECTIONS

1. Typical posterolateral disc → traversing root and radicular pattern. 2. Pars stress fracture → adolescent repetitive extension and Scotty-dog collar. 3. Spinal stenosis → compressed neural spaces, often degenerative. 4. Valve-free vertebral venous plexus → possible metastatic/infectious spread.
